beats.narration_text: On October fourteenth, I asked Claude to shorten one subtitle line, so a viewer could read it in time. It fit. It kept both negatives. And it still shifted the tone of what the character said.

beats.speaker: DEEPAK
beats.narration_text: Anyone who ships subtitles. Streaming platforms set hard limits on how fast a line can be read, and delivery guides say files that break them get sent back. In the tools I checked, shortening a line is still something a person does, one line at a time.

beats.speaker: DEEPAK
beats.narration_text: So CueGate is the tool I'm going to build. You give it a subtitle file and the film. It will hand back a file where every line fits the rules, and anything it can't fix safely will go back to a person, with the reason.

beats.narration_text: Partly. Subtitle Edit and Editsub both have an AI action that shortens the line you're on. EZTitles runs automated checks that flag reading-speed problems. In all three, a person picks the line and decides.

beats.speaker: DEEPAK
beats.narration_text: Researchers have worked on length too. In 2019, a team in Trento and at Amazon showed a translation model can be steered to write shorter output. In 2020, a Trento team found that for subtitles, hitting forty-two characters isn't enough. Timing and the rhythm of speech matter too.

beats.speaker: DEEPAK
beats.narration_text: What they got was shorter text. What none of the tools I checked publish is how often that shortening changes meaning. That's the gap CueGate will go after: a gate over the whole file, and a number you can check.

beats.speaker: DEEPAK
beats.narration_text: First, the data. The English subtitles of Tears of Steel, an open Blender film. The film is Creative Commons, but the subtitle file's own licence isn't stated, so I'll confirm it before it goes in the repo. If I can't, I'll write my own dialogue and label it synthetic. Clean files rarely break rules, so I'll squeeze their timing on purpose. That gives me failures where I still know the original line.

beats.speaker: DEEPAK
beats.narration_text: Then the pipeline. Read the file and turn every time into exact frames. Check every rule. Fix timing first, because that changes no words. Only the lines timing can't save go to a small open model running on my laptop, with an exact character budget and a list of words it must keep. Every answer comes back through the same checker.

beats.speaker: DEEPAK
beats.narration_text: No API key, and none needed to start: the rule checks and timing fixes need no model. Compute is my sixteen-inch MacBook Pro, M3 Pro, thirty-six gigabytes of memory, no cloud. The subtitle licence isn't confirmed; synthetic dialogue is the fallback. The models will be public models that download and run locally. I'll pick small ones here, after freeing disk space.

beats.speaker: DEEPAK
beats.narration_text: I'll run four versions on the same lines. A dumb cut at the budget. A single "shorten this" call to the same model. CueGate without its meaning check. And full CueGate. Then I'll label a hundred shortened lines myself, without knowing which version wrote them.

beats.speaker: DEEPAK
beats.narration_text: It worked if full CueGate ships zero rule breaks, and changes meaning less often than that single call. It failed if it changes meaning just as often, however clean the timing looks. And if it sends most lines back to a person, it saved nobody any time. I'll report that as a failure too.
